paragraphs.source_en: Okō kept writing, crossing things out and revising them as she went. The box was adorned with peacock feathers, while the jewels Ōkubo Chōan had given her were set among inlaid mother-of-pearl, each vying with the other in brilliance; its dazzling splendor made the eyes swim. As agreed, one of the two boxes had naturally gone to Chōan, while she had kept the other for herself. Now her box sat in the sunlight beneath the study window, enjoying the warmth of spring before anything else in the room.

paragraphs.source_en: News that Chōan had fallen ill had passed from the retired shogun in Sunpu to the shogun's government in Edo, as well as to the residences of Ōkubo Sagami-no-kami and Matsudaira Tadateru. No visitor was permitted to enter his room, and even his lawful wife, Lady Ikeda, believed him gravely ill. Lady Ikeda was the daughter of Ikeda Yoritatsu, a close confidant of the Honganji prelate Kennyo, and belonged to the clan of Ikeda Terumasa. If Chōan maintained the deception even before Lady Ikeda, then his concubines and children presumably knew nothing of the truth either.
